# Probability Generating Function Determines the Probability Distribution

**Theorem.** Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables whose codomains are subsets of
$\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$, and let $\Pi_X$ and $\Pi_Y$ be their probability generating
functions. Then
$$\forall s \in [-1,1] : \Pi_X(s) = \Pi_Y(s) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb{N} : \Pr(X = k) = \Pr(Y = k).$$

The claim as stated is **true**; we prove it.

---

## 0. Conventions and set-up

Throughout, $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$, and we use the standard convention $s^0 := 1$ for
**every** real $s$, including $s = 0$. (This is the convention under which the constant term of a
power series is its value at the origin; it is also the convention implicit in writing
$\Pi_X(s) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \Pr(X=k)\,s^k$.)

Let $X$ be defined on a probability space $(\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr)$ and let $Y$ be defined on a
probability space $(\Omega', \Sigma', \Pr')$; the two need not coincide, and we write $\Pr$ for both
measures when no confusion arises. Since $X$ is a discrete random variable, each set
$\{X = k\} := X^{-1}(\{k\})$ is an event, and we put
$$p_k := \Pr(X = k), \qquad q_k := \Pr(Y = k) \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

**(0.1) The sequences $(p_k)$ and $(q_k)$ are non-negative and sum to $1$.**
Clearly $p_k \ge 0$. The events $\{X = k\}$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, are pairwise disjoint (a point
$\omega$ cannot satisfy $X(\omega) = k$ and $X(\omega) = l$ for $k \ne l$), and because the codomain
of $X$ is contained in $\mathbb{N}$ we have $X(\omega) \in \mathbb{N}$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$,
so $\bigcup_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \{X = k\} = \Omega$. As $\mathbb{N}$ is countable, countable
additivity of $\Pr$ gives
$$\sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} p_k = \Pr(\Omega) = 1 . \tag{0.1}$$
The same holds for $(q_k)$. In particular $\sum_k p_k$ and $\sum_k q_k$ are convergent series of
non-negative terms, hence absolutely convergent, and the order of summation is immaterial; we fix
the increasing order of $k$ once and for all.

**(0.2) The probability generating function.** By definition
$\Pi_X(s) = \mathsf{E}\!\left[s^X\right]$. For a discrete random variable $X$ with values in
$\mathbb{N}$ and a function $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$, the expectation $\mathsf{E}[g(X)]$
exists and equals $\sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} g(k) \Pr(X = k)$ precisely when the latter series
converges absolutely. Taking $g(k) = s^k$ with $|s| \le 1$, we have $|s^k| \le 1$ and hence
$$\sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \left| s^k \right| p_k \ \le\ \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} p_k = 1 < \infty,$$
so the expectation exists and
$$\Pi_X(s) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} p_k s^k \qquad \text{for every } s \in [-1,1], \tag{0.2}$$
the series being absolutely convergent. (No issue of fractional powers arises, since $X$ takes
integer values; this is exactly why negative $s$ is admissible.) Likewise
$\Pi_Y(s) = \sum_{k} q_k s^k$ on $[-1,1]$. Thus both sides of the asserted equivalence are
meaningful.

The whole theorem is therefore a statement about real power series with absolutely summable
coefficients. We isolate the two facts we need.

---

## 1. Lemma 1 (uniform convergence and continuity on $[-1,1]$)

**Lemma 1.** Let $(c_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of real numbers with
$\sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} |c_k| < \infty$. Then the series
$$F(s) := \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} c_k s^k$$
converges absolutely for every $s \in [-1,1]$, converges uniformly on $[-1,1]$, and its sum $F$ is
continuous on $[-1,1]$.

*Proof.* For $s \in [-1,1]$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we have $|s|^k \le 1$ (for $k = 0$ this reads
$|s^0| = 1 \le 1$, by our convention). Hence
$$\left| c_k s^k \right| \le |c_k| =: M_k \qquad \text{for all } s \in [-1,1].$$
Since $\sum_k M_k = \sum_k |c_k| < \infty$, the Weierstrass $M$-test applies: the series
$\sum_k c_k s^k$ converges absolutely for each $s \in [-1,1]$ and converges uniformly on $[-1,1]$.

The partial sums $F_N(s) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} c_k s^k$ are polynomials, hence continuous on $[-1,1]$.
A uniform limit of continuous real-valued functions on a metric space is continuous; therefore $F$
is continuous on $[-1,1]$. $\blacksquare$

Note that Lemma 1 applies to $(p_k)$ and to $(q_k)$ by $(0.1)$, and also to the difference sequence
$(p_k - q_k)$, since $\sum_k |p_k - q_k| \le \sum_k p_k + \sum_k q_k = 2 < \infty$.

---

## 2. Lemma 2 (an elementary identity theorem)

**Lemma 2.** Let $(c_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be real with $\sum_{k} |c_k| < \infty$, and let
$F(s) = \sum_{k} c_k s^k$ for $s \in [-1,1]$ (well defined by Lemma 1). Let
$S \subseteq (0,1]$ be a set having $0$ as an accumulation point, i.e. for every $\delta > 0$ there
exists $s \in S$ with $0 < s < \delta$. If
$$F(s) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } s \in S,$$
then $c_k = 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

*Proof.* We prove by induction on $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the statement
$$P(n) : \qquad c_0 = c_1 = \dots = c_{n-1} = 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ c_n = 0 ,$$
where for $n = 0$ the hypothesis is vacuous (there are no indices $j < 0$), so $P(0)$ asserts simply
$c_0 = 0$. Establishing $P(n)$ for all $n$ yields, by (strong) induction, that $c_n = 0$ for all
$n$: indeed, if $c_j = 0$ for all $j < n$ then $P(n)$ gives $c_n = 0$, and the case $n = 0$ starts
the induction.

So fix $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and assume $c_j = 0$ for all $j < n$.

**Step 1: the tail series.** Define $b_j := c_{n+j}$ for $j \in \mathbb{N}$. Then
$$\sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}} |b_j| = \sum_{k \ge n} |c_k| \le \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} |c_k| < \infty,$$
(the middle equality because $k \mapsto n+k$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{N}$ onto $\{k : k \ge n\}$,
and all terms are non-negative). Hence by Lemma 1 the function
$$G(s) := \sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}} b_j s^j = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}} c_{n+j}\, s^{j}$$
is defined and continuous on $[-1,1]$, and — using $s^0 = 1$ at $s = 0$, while $0^j = 0$ for
$j \ge 1$ — its value at the origin is
$$G(0) = b_0 = c_n. \tag{2.1}$$

**Step 2: factorisation.** Let $s \in [-1,1]$ with $s \ne 0$. For $N \ge n$, the induction hypothesis
$c_0 = \dots = c_{n-1} = 0$ gives
$$F_N(s) := \sum_{k=0}^{N} c_k s^k = \sum_{k=n}^{N} c_k s^k = s^n \sum_{j=0}^{N-n} c_{n+j} s^{j}
= s^n\, G_{N-n}(s),$$
where $G_m(s) := \sum_{j=0}^{m} b_j s^j$; the middle equality is the substitution $k = n + j$ in a
*finite* sum, and the factor $s^n$ may be pulled out of a finite sum. Letting $N \to \infty$ (so that
$N - n \to \infty$) and using that both $F_N(s) \to F(s)$ and $G_{N-n}(s) \to G(s)$ converge, together
with the fact that multiplication by the constant $s^n$ is continuous, we obtain
$$F(s) = s^n\, G(s) \qquad \text{for all } s \in [-1,1] \setminus \{0\}. \tag{2.2}$$

**Step 3: conclusion.** Let $s \in S$. Then $s \in (0,1]$, so $s \ne 0$ and $s^n > 0$. By hypothesis
$F(s) = 0$, so $(2.2)$ gives $s^n G(s) = 0$ and therefore
$$G(s) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } s \in S. \tag{2.3}$$
Since $0$ is an accumulation point of $S$, for each $m \in \mathbb{N}$ we may choose
$s_m \in S$ with $0 < s_m < \tfrac{1}{m+1}$; then $s_m \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$, and $s_m \in [-1,1]$.
By continuity of $G$ at $0$ (Step 1) and by $(2.3)$,
$$c_n \overset{(2.1)}{=} G(0) = \lim_{m \to \infty} G(s_m) = \lim_{m \to \infty} 0 = 0 .$$
This proves $P(n)$, and the induction is complete. $\blacksquare$

---

## 3. Proof of the Theorem

Recall $p_k = \Pr(X = k)$, $q_k = \Pr(Y = k)$, and that by $(0.2)$
$$\Pi_X(s) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} p_k s^k, \qquad
  \Pi_Y(s) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} q_k s^k \qquad (s \in [-1,1]),$$
both series converging absolutely.

### 3.1 ($\Leftarrow$) Equal PMFs imply equal PGFs

Suppose $p_k = q_k$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Fix $s \in [-1,1]$. Then $p_k s^k = q_k s^k$ for
every $k$, so the two series $\sum_k p_k s^k$ and $\sum_k q_k s^k$ have identical terms, hence
identical partial sums, hence (both being convergent) identical sums:
$$\Pi_X(s) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} p_k s^k = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} q_k s^k = \Pi_Y(s).$$
As $s \in [-1,1]$ was arbitrary, $\Pi_X = \Pi_Y$ on $[-1,1]$.

### 3.2 ($\Rightarrow$) Equal PGFs imply equal PMFs

Suppose $\Pi_X(s) = \Pi_Y(s)$ for all $s \in [-1,1]$. Put
$$a_k := p_k - q_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$
By $(0.1)$ and the triangle inequality,
$$\sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} |a_k| \ \le\ \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} p_k + \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} q_k = 1 + 1 = 2 < \infty ,$$
so $(a_k)$ satisfies the hypothesis of Lemmas 1 and 2. Let
$$F(s) := \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} a_k s^k \qquad (s \in [-1,1]),$$
which is well defined by Lemma 1. For each fixed $s \in [-1,1]$ the series $\sum_k p_k s^k$ and
$\sum_k q_k s^k$ both converge, so by linearity of convergent series (termwise subtraction of two
convergent series is legitimate and the sums subtract)
$$F(s) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \left( p_k s^k - q_k s^k \right)
      = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} p_k s^k - \sum_{k \in \mathbb{N}} q_k s^k
      = \Pi_X(s) - \Pi_Y(s) = 0 .$$
Thus $F$ vanishes identically on $[-1,1]$, and in particular on the set
$$S := \left(0, 1\right) \subseteq (0,1],$$
which certainly has $0$ as an accumulation point. By Lemma 2, $a_k = 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
that is,
$$\Pr(X = k) = p_k = q_k = \Pr(Y = k) \qquad \text{for all } k \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Both implications are proved, so the equivalence holds. $\blacksquare$

---

## 4. Remarks

**4.1 (What was actually used).** The proof of $(\Rightarrow)$ used the hypothesis only on a subset
of $(0,1]$ accumulating at $0$. Hence the following sharper statement holds, with the same proof:
*if $S \subseteq (0,1]$ has $0$ as an accumulation point and $\Pi_X(s) = \Pi_Y(s)$ for all $s \in S$,
then $X$ and $Y$ have the same probability mass function.* For instance, agreement of the two PGFs
at the single sequence of points $s = 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, \dots$ already forces equality of the
distributions. Conversely, one cannot dispense with an accumulation point at $0$ in this elementary
formulation: agreement at finitely many points says nothing.

**4.2 (Why $[-1,1]$).** The restriction $|s| \le 1$ is what guarantees that $\mathsf{E}[s^X]$ exists
for *every* distribution on $\mathbb{N}$, via $\sum_k p_k |s|^k \le \sum_k p_k = 1$. For $|s| > 1$
the defining series may diverge (e.g. $p_k = c/(k^2 2^k)$ gives a PGF with radius of convergence $2$;
heavier tails give radius exactly $1$), so $[-1,1]$ is the largest interval on which the PGF of an
arbitrary $\mathbb{N}$-valued random variable is guaranteed to be defined.

**4.3 (Relation to the analytic identity theorem).** Lemma 2 is an elementary, self-contained
substitute for the standard identity theorem for power series. Alternatively, one may invoke the
theorem that a power series with radius of convergence $R > 0$ is infinitely differentiable on
$(-R, R)$ with $c_k = F^{(k)}(0)/k!$; since here $\sum |c_k| < \infty$ forces $R \ge 1$, and
$F \equiv 0$ on $(-1,1)$ forces all derivatives at $0$ to vanish, one again gets $c_k = 0$. Applied
to $\Pi_X$ itself this yields the useful inversion formula
$$\Pr(X = k) = \frac{\Pi_X^{(k)}(0)}{k!} \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}),$$
which exhibits the PMF explicitly as a functional of the PGF and thereby re-proves $(\Rightarrow)$.
We preferred the argument of Lemma 2 because it needs nothing beyond the Weierstrass $M$-test and
the continuity of uniform limits.

**4.4 (Indexing convention).** If one prefers the convention $\mathbb{N} = \{1,2,3,\dots\}$, the
statement and proof are unaffected: simply set $p_0 := 0 =: q_0$ and run the identical argument over
$\{0,1,2,\dots\}$; the conclusion $a_k = 0$ for all $k \ge 0$ contains the desired conclusion for
all $k \ge 1$.

**4.5 (Generality).** Nothing required $X$ and $Y$ to be defined on a common probability space, nor
required their ranges to be infinite; a random variable with finite range is covered, its $p_k$
being eventually $0$.
